primary.thesis: The two leaders have not met in person since the Paris Normandy-format summit in December 2019. Through every round of talks since 2022 (Istanbul, the Gulf-mediated contacts, the US-brokered process), the Kremlin has kept the same position. Putin will meet Zelenskyy only to sign a deal that is already finished at the technical level. Moscow also keeps questioning whether Zelenskyy has the legitimacy to sign anything. Only three months remain in the window. For a meeting to happen, a full settlement would have to be negotiated, the security-guarantee and territory questions agreed, and a venue arranged, all before 31 December 2026. The most likely outcome is 'No meeting before 2027'. If a meeting did happen, the likeliest hosts would be neutral mediators: Turkey, the Gulf states or the US. The venues on the list that Kyiv would never accept can be shorted. Zelenskyy would not go to Russia (including occupied territory) or to Belarus, and Putin would not go to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

basket.reason: The core thesis. There has been no in-person meeting in almost seven years, the Kremlin demands that a signable deal exists first, and little calendar time is left.
Even if a meeting happens, Zelenskyy travelling to Moscow or to occupied territory would amount to political capitulation, and his security there could not be guaranteed. Kyiv would not accept it.
Belarus is a co-belligerent. Russian forces used its territory to invade in 2022, so Kyiv rejects Minsk as a venue.
Putin will not travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory. Under the rules, a meeting in occupied Ukraine counts as Russia, not Ukraine.

failure_narrative: The basket loses mainly if a ceasefire or framework peace agreement comes together quickly in Q4 2026. The likeliest trigger is sustained US pressure, for example threats of secondary sanctions on buyers of Russian oil together with conditional sanction relief. That pressure could combine with Russian economic strain and front-line exhaustion to produce a signing summit, most likely in Istanbul, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi/Doha or a US location, with the American president present. In that world C11 goes to zero. The three NO legs still pay unless the meeting is held in Minsk, in Moscow or in occupied territory. A secondary way to lose: Kyiv accepts a Russian-controlled venue as a humiliating condition of a deal under battlefield collapse.
hedge_thesis: The worlds where the primary fails are worlds with a real settlement in progress, and a settlement would show up in European energy and defense markets. A Putin–Zelenskyy meeting would be the capstone of a ceasefire and sanctions-easing framework. Markets would then price three things. First, Russian pipeline gas and LNG might partly return and the risk to Black Sea shipping would ease, so Dutch TTF gas and European power prices would fall. Second, the urgency of European rearmament would fade, so the European defense names that rose on the war (Rheinmetall and peers) would sell off. Third, Ukrainian sovereign bonds and GDP warrants would rally on reconstruction financing, and grain prices would drop as Black Sea corridor risk premia disappear. A position that gains from falling European gas prices, weaker EU defense stocks or stronger Ukrainian bonds would therefore pay in exactly the worlds where 'No meeting before 2027' fails.
